description: We are building an public-facing web tool to display images of the sky from the SPHEREx mission, making it easy for anyone to quickly see how they change over time. Users will enter the coordinates of a patch of sky (Right Ascension and declination). Your tool will display a series of images of that patch like a little video, making it easy to spot moving objects.
summary:
Planet X - SPHEREx Explorer, a light, portable web tool for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 "Planet X and SPHEREx" challenge. You enter an object name (for example Barnard's Star) or sky coordinates (RA/Dec). The tool finds every matching real NASA SPHEREx infrared image in the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA) and plays them as a time-lapse "blink" video of that patch of sky.
Our tool covers each part of the brief:
   - Coordinate and name input, with shareable URLs that reproduce a view exactly
   - A data pipeline that queries and streams SPHEREx multi-extension FITS files from IRSA.
   - Band management: a 102-channel wavelength slider and detector (D1-D6) selection.
   - Difference imaging that subtracts epochs (-Static, -First, -Prev) so moving objects stand out.
   We ran the full pipeline on the live archive for all five mandatory test targets.
SPHEREx maps the entire sky in 102 infrared colours every six months, but its data are huge (about 65 MB per FITS file) and hard for non-specialists to use. WiseView, the similar tool for the earlier WISE mission, let the public make hundreds of discoveries of brown dwarfs and nearby cold objects. Our tool gives everyone the same ability with SPHEREx data: students, citizen scientists and astronomers can search for a hidden "Planet X", nearby brown dwarfs, asteroids, high-proper-motion stars and variable stars.
details:
a. What it does and how it works:

- Input and resolution: names are resolved through CDS Sesame (SIMBAD) with mirror fallbacks. Coordinates can be decimal or sexagesimal. The target's position is propagated with its proper motion to the SPHEREx observing date.

- Archive query: the Python (FastAPI) backend queries IRSA's IVOA SIA v2 service for SPHEREx DR1 (and QR) exposures that cover the position.

- Efficient data reading: instead of downloading whole 65 MB files, the backend uses HTTP range requests. It reads only the header, the WCS-WAVE wavelength table and the pixel rows/columns it needs, about 35-60 KB per exposure, verified bit-identical to the official cutouts.

- Processing: each exposure is reprojected north-up using its full SIP-distortion WCS, and the background (zodiacal light) is removed with a clipped median. Exposures are grouped into epochs (visits about 6 months apart). Each epoch is stacked per detector with inverse-variance weights and outlier (cosmic-ray) rejection, and every epoch uses the same detector set, so brightness changes are real.

- Spectrum: clicking a source runs aperture photometry on every exposure. SPHEREx's linear-variable filters give each exposure a different wavelength at that spot, and the results are binned into the 102 official channels.

- Context: Gaia DR3, AllWISE and CatWISE2020 sources are drawn on the frames, propagated to each frame's date, with motion arrows. An optional Aladin Lite sky atlas shows DSS2, 2MASS, AllWISE and the SPHEREx DR1 cube.

- Metadata and flags: for each frame the tool shows dates, detectors, wavelengths, sky background, noise, coverage and the rejected-pixel fraction.

b. Benefits:

- Uses real, current NASA SPHEREx data streamed live.

- Very low resources: about 82 MB of RAM idle and about 140 MB peak while processing 200 exposures. A 160-exposure query reads only 5-10 MB of data.

- Portable: one click to start, only 5 Python packages, no build tools.

- Fast: repeat queries take 3-8 seconds thanks to disk and memory caches.

- Scientifically careful: consistent band weighting, quality flags, proper-motion propagation, and an automated validation script for the mandatory targets.

- Reproducible and shareable: URLs encode the full view, including display settings.

c. Intended impact:

- Open SPHEREx's all-sky, 102-band infrared survey to the public the way WiseView opened WISE, so that citizen scientists can discover new brown dwarfs, cold nearby objects, asteroids, high-proper-motion stars and variable stars.

- Give students and educators a hands-on way to see stellar motion, variability and infrared spectra in real NASA data.

- Give researchers a quick way to check any position for motion, variability and spectral shape before deeper analysis.

d. Tools used:

- Backend: Python 3.10+, FastAPI, Uvicorn, Astropy, NumPy, httpx.

- Frontend: plain HTML5, CSS and JavaScript ES modules, HTML5 Canvas for the image viewer, spectrum chart and animated galaxy background, MediaRecorder for WebM export.

- Sky atlas: Aladin Lite v3 (CDS), loaded on demand.

- Data services and protocols: NASA/IPAC IRSA SIA v2 (IVOA standard), the IRSA SPHEREx data server and its AWS S3 mirror, CDS Sesame/SIMBAD, VizieR mirrors (CDS, Harvard CfA, IDIA), and IRSA HiPS surveys.

e. How the project is creative:

- Partial FITS reads: the tool reads only the needed bytes of each 65 MB SPHEREx file instead of using the cutout service, which returns about 4 MB per cutout. It even decodes the RICE-compressed FLAGS extension from only the tiles it needs. This is about 100 times less data.

- "-Static" difference mode subtracts the per-pixel median of all frames, so fixed stars cancel and moving objects appear as black/white pairs.

- Catalogue overlays propagated to each frame's own date, so you can see whether a source moves the way Gaia or CatWISE predict.

- The automatic warning for stale coordinates helps users avoid looking at an empty patch of sky.

f. Factors our team considered:

- Scientific accuracy: correct WCS/SIP reprojection, consistent detector mix across epochs, saturation handling, proper motion, and per-exposure wavelengths from each file's own spectral WCS.

- Performance and accessibility on low-end hardware: low RAM, CPU and bandwidth, small page size, lazy loading.

- Reliability: mirror fallbacks for every external service, retries, protection against accidentally downloading whole 65 MB files, and offline presets for the mandatory targets.

- Ease of use: one-click start, presets, keyboard shortcuts, help, shareable links, and layouts for desktop and mobile.

- Rules and attribution: no NASA branding or logos in the interface, and data credited to NASA/JPL-Caltech/IPAC, ESA/DPAC and CDS.
